title: What would it take to change your mind?
author: Craig Barton
summary: Responding to pushback on his earlier newsletters, Craig Barton makes the case for asking, of any educational belief, what evidence would change your mind. He applies the test to his own advocacy of mini-whiteboards, recounting a coaching observation where a teacher could not say how many students had understood the We Do, and a follow-up lesson where Step-by-Step whiteboard checks let her name exactly who had gone wrong. He would drop mini-whiteboards if teachers without them knew their students' understanding just as well. He then applies it to setting versus mixed-attainment teaching, describing the school-comparison evidence he would accept, and contrasts this with a colleague for whom nothing could change her view. His argument is that beliefs which cannot be refuted cannot be tested, and he challenges readers to state their own.
points: Barton proposes that every strongly held teaching belief should come with a stated condition under which it would be abandoned.
His coaching example shows why he values mini-whiteboards: a teacher who could not say who understood the We Do later identified the exact three students after using Step-by-Step.
He specifies the evidence that would overturn his preference for setting: consistently better Progress 8 maths results in comparable mixed-attainment schools.
A colleague who said nothing would change her mind about mixed-attainment teaching illustrates the unfalsifiable belief he considers a problem.
He ends with a reader challenge to name a deep belief, the reasons for it, and what would change it.
quotes: Let’s take mini-whiteboards. I love them. In all the school support work I have done over the last five years, I have advocated using them throughout each phase of a maths lesson.

During her We Do - the topic was expanding double brackets - she Cold-Called five students to help construct the solution and then asked if anyone was stuck or had any questions. There was silence, so she set the students off on consolidation work.

Longer-term, if I observed more teachers who did not use mini-whiteboards during the We Do and yet had a good sense of their students’ understanding, I would change my mind. I would no longer see them as an essential tool during this phase of a lesson and instead seek to learn how these teachers were gathering such information.

I would then compare their Progress 8 scores for maths, drilling down into the scores of both higher and lower prior attaining students. If mixed-attainment schools consistently outperformed schools that teach in sets, I would change my mind.
She said that nothing would. She believed with all her heart in mixed-attainment teaching, and for her, that was all that mattered.
However, I am prepared to change my deep-rooted beliefs based on evidence. I am not sure that is true of some of the teachers I meet (or who email me in response to my newsletters).
